title: Teaching
text: Theory disciplines the evidence, the evidence tests the theory, and students learn best when they work with both. In my courses, students read the research behind the textbook and then make a case of their own—taking a country’s development record, for instance, and defending a policy response before the class.

title: Teaching
text:
Old Courses
ECON 104: Principles of Macroeconomics Summer 2024; Summer 2023
An introduction to thinking like an economist about the whole economy, built around a few big questions: why some nations are rich and others poor, what the Federal Reserve does, and why economies go through business cycles.
ECON 306: Intermediate Microeconomics Fall 2023
Price theory at the intermediate level: consumer choice and demand, production and costs, and how market structure shapes prices and output, practiced through weekly problem sets with an emphasis on graphical analysis.
ECON 360: Economics of Developing Areas Spring 2023, Fall 2022, Summer 2022
Why are some countries rich and others poor? The course moves from Malthus and Solow through poverty traps, the aid debate, health and human capital, institutions, culture, state capacity, and conflict, pairing Easterly, Banerjee and Duflo, and Koyama and Rubin with research by North, Nunn, Dell, and others. Students write discussion essays and present a country case.
ECON 385: International Economic Policy Spring 2022, Fall 2021
The economic way of thinking applied to trade and international finance, including introductory microeconomics and game theory, with historical and current evidence on the consequences of trade, protectionism, and conflict. Taught for non-major students.

title: About Me
text:
I am an Economics PhD student at George Mason University. I received my bachelor’s in Economics from GMU in 2019 and my master’s in 2021. 
I am on the 2026–27 academic job market. My CV and the Research page list my current papers and drafts.
My research interests include political and applied microeconomics, historical political economy, growth, and institutional change. Of particular focus are periods of conflict and how individual behavior is shaped by those conditions. I work primarily in R and Python, and have experience with geospatial analysis, text-as-data methods, and historical data digitization. I have taught undergraduate courses as a graduate lecturer at George Mason University, including microeconomics, macroeconomics, and international development.
I hope that my work will help build a greater understanding of the social and political questions of the past and today. Outside of academia, I enjoy reading sci-fi/fantasy, playing the latest strategy games, and traveling with my partner.

Late Medieval Unrest in the Holy Roman Empire: Climate, Institutions, and Documented Unrest Draft






NoneAbstract





I link a geolocated, event-level catalog of popular unrest to an annual panel of city-council representation across 301 cities of the Holy Roman Empire, 1300–1520, dating unrest against institutional change and climate shocks. Guild representation’s apparent associations with unrest come from the years in which representation changed, often in the course of unrest; coded at each century’s start, the same panel makes guild seats appear to lower unrest. Away from those years neither guild nor burgher representation shows a clear association with unrest. Contrary to the closest published study, documented unrest is, if anything, more frequent in wetter years. The divergence lies in the catalogs, which barely overlap; on that study’s own data, its drought and muting estimates for outbreaks in the Empire are not significant once a year’s conflict starts may share a shock. Every association is descriptive.



Did Newspaper Competition Promote Rebellion? The Case of the 1837-38 Rebellions in Quebec Draft Appendix SSRN

with Vincent Geloso







NoneAbstract





We study the relationship between media competition and political mobilization during the Quebec Rebellion of 1837–38. Using a new spatial dataset of newspaper agents, we test whether local press competition increased rebel activity independently of newspaper ideology. We find that greater media competition strongly predicts mobilization, especially in areas where seigneurial tenure persisted, suggesting that concentrated grievances became politically activated through competitive information networks. The results remain robust after controlling for literacy and school enrollment. Overall, competitive media transformed latent discontent into active rebelliousness.




ProMarket: How Newspaper Competition Fueled Quebec’s 1837 Rebellion

The Specter of Slavery: Election Timing and the Campaign Agenda in the Party Press, 1860–1864 Draft






NoneAbstract





Was slavery’s place in the Northern press of 1860 set by the election campaign or by the news? A keyword dictionary applied to six million newspaper articles traces slavery coverage around the staggered congressional elections of 1860–1864. In the 1860 cycle, coverage fell after the vote by about two-fifths of its normal level, net of trend, along with campaign and tariff coverage, while the rest of the non-campaign agenda held steady. The drop followed each state’s own election date rather than the national calendar. It did not recur in 1862 and was smaller and not significant in 1864, when the campaigns turned on the war rather than on slavery’s extension. Within cities, Democratic papers used the vocabulary of racial equality more often than their Republican rivals, most clearly in 1864. Slavery behaved as campaign material at the margin of a persistent debate that did not follow the vote.
